candidates.workingClaim: February 1, 1960: On February 1, 1960, four African Americans began a sit-in at a segregated Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, a protest that helped spark sit-ins across the American South.
February 1, 1896: On February 1, 1896, Giacomo Puccini's opera La Boheme had its premiere at the Teatro Regio in Turin, Italy.
February 1, 1946: On February 1, 1946, the Norwegian politician and diplomat Trygve Lie was elected the first secretary-general of the United Nations.
February 1, 2003: On February 1, 2003, the US space shuttle Columbia broke up at an altitude of about 40 miles (60 km) over Texas while returning to Earth, killing all seven crew members.
February 1, 2009: On February 1, 2009, Johanna Sigurdardottir was sworn in as prime minister of Iceland, the first woman to hold the post.
February 2, 1887: On February 2, 1887, a group in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, went looking for a groundhog to predict the weather, beginning the town's Groundhog Day tradition.
February 2, 1848: On February 2, 1848, the United States and Mexico signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, ending the Mexican-American War.

February 2, 1990: On February 2, 1990, South African President F.W. de Klerk lifted the 30-year ban on the African National Congress, leading to Nelson Mandela's release from prison and marking the beginning of the end of apartheid.
February 2, 1943: On February 2, 1943, the Battle of Stalingrad ended with the surrender of German troops to the Soviet army, a turning point of World War II.
February 2, 1882: On February 2, 1882, the Irish writer James Joyce, author of Ulysses, was born in Dublin.
February 3, 1995: On February 3, 1995, the American astronaut Eileen Collins became the first woman to pilot a space shuttle, flying aboard Discovery.
February 3, 1870: On February 3, 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment to the US Constitution was ratified, guaranteeing Americans the right to vote regardless of race.
February 3, 1809: On February 3, 1809, the German composer Felix Mendelssohn was born. He largely followed Classical models while helping to shape Romanticism.
February 3, 1975: On February 3, 1975, the Egyptian singer Umm Kulthum, one of the most famous Arab singers and public figures of the 20th century, died in Cairo.
February 3, 1959: On February 3, 1959, the American rock 'n' roll singer Buddy Holly was killed in a plane crash at age 22.
February 4, 2004: On February 4, 2004, Harvard students Mark Zuckerberg, Eduardo Saverin, Dustin Moskovitz and Chris Hughes founded and launched the website TheFacebook.com, which became Facebook.
February 4, 1948: On February 4, 1948, Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, gained independence from Great Britain, which had controlled the island since 1796.
February 4, 1945: On February 4, 1945, in the final stages of World War II, the Yalta Conference opened with Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Joseph Stalin.
February 4, 1789: On February 4, 1789, George Washington was elected the first president of the United States by a unanimous vote of the first electoral college.
February 4, 1932: On February 4, 1932, the United States hosted its first Winter Olympic Games, in Lake Placid, New York.
February 5, 1917: On February 5, 1917, Mexico adopted its present constitution, which holds that the government should take an active role in the country's day-to-day affairs.

February 5, 1900: On February 5, 1900, the United States and Great Britain signed the first Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, concerning a projected Central American canal. The US Senate declined to ratify it, and a second treaty in 1901 gave the United States a free hand.
February 5, 1971: On February 5, 1971, Apollo 14's lunar module landed in the Fra Mauro highlands of the Moon. Commander Alan Shepard later swung at two golf balls with a makeshift club.
February 5, 1985: On February 5, 1985, the soccer player Cristiano Ronaldo was born in Funchal, Portugal.
February 5, 2003: On February 5, 2003, US Secretary of State Colin Powell appeared before the United Nations Security Council to present evidence that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction.
February 6, 1840: On February 6, 1840, the British and Maori chiefs of the North Island signed the Treaty of Waitangi (Te Tiriti o Waitangi).
February 6, 1952: On February 6, 1952, Elizabeth II ascended the throne of the United Kingdom following the death of her father, King George VI.
February 6, 1945: On February 6, 1945, the singer-songwriter Bob Marley was born. He found stardom blending ska, rock steady and reggae.
February 6, 1895: On February 6, 1895, the baseball player Babe Ruth was born. His home-run hitting made him one of the most celebrated athletes in American sports.
February 6, 2018: On February 6, 2018, SpaceX's Falcon Heavy launch vehicle made its first test flight.
February 7, 1964: On February 7, 1964, the Beatles landed in New York City.
February 7, 1914: On February 7, 1914, Charlie Chaplin debuted his most famous screen character, the Little Tramp, in the film Kid Auto Races at Venice.
February 7, 1812: On February 7, 1812, the novelist Charles Dickens was born in Portsmouth, England.
February 7, 1974: On February 7, 1974, Grenada gained independence from the United Kingdom.
February 7, 1999: On February 7, 1999, Abdullah II became king of Jordan, hours after the death of his father, King Hussein.
